questions.question: How do you send and receive on a channel in Go?
questions.title: Send Receive Operations
questions.direct_answer: ch <- v sends v; v := <-ch receives. On an unbuffered channel both operations block until the other side is present — the send/receive meet is the synchronization.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: ch <- v sends v; v := <-ch receives.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The two operators are the whole channel interface:

```go
ch <- 42       // send 42 into ch
v := <-ch      // receive from ch into v
<-ch           // receive and discard (fire-and-forget drain)
```

Arrow points in the direction of data flow: ch <- v pushes into the channel, <-ch pulls out of it. The mnemonic: the arrow shows where the value goes.

On an unbuffered channel, each operation is half of a rendezvous. The send blocks until a receiver is ready; the receive blocks until a sender is. Whichever happens first waits; when the second arrives, the value transfers and both continue. That blocking IS the feature — it's why an unbuffered send returning is proof that someone received.

On a buffered channel: the send only blocks when the buffer is full; the receive only blocks when the buffer is empty. Values queue in between — the buffer absorbs the timing gap.

The operators also compose into other syntax: `v, ok := <-ch` (comma-ok — ok is false if the channel is closed and drained), and `for v := range ch` (receive until close). Those forms cover the three questions a receiver has: give me a value, is this channel still alive, and give me everything until it's done.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Under the operators: both send and receive take the channel's lock, check the wait queues, and either complete on the fast path or park. The interesting mechanics are the two rendezvous cases:

Sender arrives, no receiver, buffer full: the sender goroutine is parked, and — this is the elegant part — the VALUE it's sending is parked WITH it: the runtime copies the value into the sender goroutine's own stack slot and links that goroutine into the channel's send queue. When a receiver later arrives, it locks the channel, finds a parked sender, copies the value directly from the sender's stack into the receiver's result — goroutine-to-goroutine, buffer never involved.

Receiver arrives first, no sender: parks on the recv queue with a pointer to its own stack slot for the eventual copy. When a sender arrives on a channel with waiting receivers, the value copies straight sender→receiver, bypassing the buffer even on a buffered channel.

Those two direct paths explain the performance folklore: an unbuffered channel send+receive pair is one copy and two lock operations — the 'rendezvous' is literally two stacks meeting through the channel's lock, and the value is copied once. A buffered send+receive is two copies (sender→buffer, buffer→receiver) but the two sides never have to be scheduled together. That's the mechanical trade: unbuffered trades a scheduling dependency for one fewer copy.

questions.question: What does v, ok := <-ch do, and when is ok false?
questions.title: When would you use Send Receive Operations in a real project
questions.direct_answer: ok is false only when the channel is closed AND the buffer is drained. It distinguishes 'a real zero value' from 'channel finished'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Send Receive Operations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: ok is false only when the channel is closed AND the buffer is drained.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The comma-ok form answers the receiver's real question — is this channel still live?

```go
v, ok := <-ch
```

ok is true: a value was received (v holds it — even if v is the zero value of the type, because someone SENT a zero). ok is false: the channel is closed and there are no more values — v is the zero value as a placeholder, not data.

The case it exists for: a channel of ints where 0 is legitimate data. Without ok, a closed-drained channel and a channel that sent 0 are indistinguishable — both give v == 0. With ok, the two cases split.

The mechanics of 'closed and drained': after close, buffered values are STILL received normally (ok true for each buffered value). Only when the buffer is empty do receives start returning (zero, false). Executed: send 10 into a buffered channel, close it, receive twice — first gives (10, true), second gives (0, false).

So ok false means exactly: no more values will ever arrive. That makes it the loop-until-done primitive when range doesn't fit (you need per-receive logic, or you're in a select):

```go
for {
    v, ok := <-ch
    if !ok {
        break // channel closed and drained
    }
    process(v)
}
```
— which is exactly what range-over-channel does for you, which is why range is the idiom and comma-ok is the explicit form.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    IN[start state] --> STEP[operation]
    STEP --> OUT[observable result]
    OUT --> EDGE[the boundary case]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The semantics have a queue-flavored subtlety worth internalizing: close doesn't 'clear' a buffered channel. The close operation is a marker placed BEHIND the buffered values. Receivers drain the buffer first (ok true), then hit the marker (ok false). The channel behaves like a queue with a tombstone at the end — FIFO delivery of everything sent before close, then a permanent end signal.

The two design decisions that matter here: receiving from a closed channel returns immediately (never blocks — the close makes the channel permanently readable as 'empty'), and receiving from a nil channel blocks forever. The three channel states (nil, open, closed) give three receive behaviors (block, normal, zero+false-or-buffered) — the complete state table:

- nil: block forever
- open, has value or sender: deliver
- open, empty: block until a sender
- closed, buffered values: deliver them
- closed, drained: zero value, ok false — immediately, forever

Every channel bug is a misreading of that table. The nil-receive-forever is the undeclared-channel bug; the closed-drained (zero, false) misread as data is the 'why am I getting zeros' bug; the closed-but-buffered (values still flowing) surprise is the 'I closed it, why is data still arriving' bug — each is one row of the table.

questions.question: What happens when you send to a closed channel?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Send Receive Operations
questions.direct_answer: Panics immediately: send on closed channel. Close is a one-way, sender-owned signal — the channel must never be sent to after close.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Send Receive Operations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: Panics immediately: send on closed channel. Close is a one-way, sender-owned signal — the channel must never be.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
It panics — immediately, on the send:

```go
ch := make(chan int, 1)
close(ch)
ch <- 1     // panic: send on closed channel
```

Executed and transcribed: the panic text is literally `send on closed channel`. Not a block, not a silent drop — a hard failure designed to be loud.

Why so harsh: close broadcasts 'no more values coming' to every receiver. A send after close would make that broadcast a lie — receivers that already observed the close and exited would have missed the late value, and the channel's FIFO-then-tombstone contract would be incoherent. Go enforces the invariant with the only mechanism that can't be ignored: the panic.

The design consequence, and the rule to take into code: exactly one owner closes, and that owner is on the SEND side. Multiple senders can't safely close (who knows no one else will send?), which is why multi-sender topologies either use a dedicated closer channel, a sync.WaitGroup before the closer, or a single fan-in goroutine that owns the close. Receivers never close: closing from the receive side races every other receiver's comma-ok — the same one-way-signal logic, mirrored.

The panic-vs-block contrast is the interview-grade point: every other invalid channel state blocks (nil) or degrades gracefully (closed reads). Only the send-after-close panics, because it's the only state that would corrupt the channel's semantic contract rather than just stall it.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics of why close-then-send panics while close-then-receive degrades: close marks the channel by closing the send-side of the state machine — a flag (closed=1) on the hchan and a wake-up broadcast to ALL parked receivers. Receivers, on waking, find the flag, and each takes either a buffered value or the (zero, false) result. The channel is permanently readable.

The send path checks the same flag first: closed → panic. No waiting, no recovery path — the check is at the top of the send, before any queueing. Because the check is under the channel lock, a send racing a close is decided atomically: either the send enqueued before close (receiver will get it — FIFO preserved) or close won (send panics). There's no interleaving where a value vanishes.

That's the same design philosophy as Go's map-concurrent-access panic: concurrent contract violations should crash LOUDLY in development rather than corrupt quietly in production. A send-after-close is almost always a lifecycle bug — some goroutine didn't get the shutdown signal — and the panic is the stack trace pointing at the goroutine that missed it.

The close protocol in one sentence, worth memorizing because it summarizes the entire ownership model: ONE sender (or an owner coordinating all senders) closes when production is complete; receivers drain via range or comma-ok; nobody sends after; nobody receives-closes. Channels with that discipline compose into pipelines that never hit the panic.

questions.question: Can you close a receive-only channel?
questions.title: compare Send Receive Operations with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: No — close is a send-side operation, and the type system forbids it: compile error on a <-chan. Closing is the sender announcing 'no more values', which a receiver has no authority to do.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Send Receive Operations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: No — close is a send-side operation, and the type system forbids it: compile error on a <-chan.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The type system answers directly:

```go
func consume(in <-chan int) {
    close(in)   // compile error: cannot close receive-only channel
}
```

The error is at compile time — the direction narrowing isn't just documentation, it's enforcement of the close ownership rule.

Why receivers can't close: close is a broadcast to all receivers that no more values are coming. A receiver closing the channel races every OTHER receiver — one consumer deciding 'we're done' while another is still waiting for a value it was promised would arrive. And it races the senders: the legitimate producer would then send-after-close — a panic — through no fault of its own logic. Close is a production-side fact ('I will never send again'), and only the producer knows it.

The pattern this forces (correctly): a consumer that's finished early doesn't close the input — it just stops reading and lets GC collect the channel when all references drop, or it signals via a SEPARATE cancellation channel (the context.Context pattern — Done() is a <-chan that the producer side closes). Cancellation and completion flow through their own channels, each closed by its owner. That separation — data channels closed by producers, cancellation channels closed by whoever owns the cancellation — is the idiom that keeps pipelines composable.

questions.question: What is the difference between a blocking send and a dropped message?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Send Receive Operations
questions.direct_answer: Go channels never drop messages — a send either blocks until delivered (or buffered) or panics on a closed channel. Dropping requires building it yourself: select with default, or a time-bounded select.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Go channels never drop messages — a send either blocks until delivered (or buffered) or panics on a closed channel.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The never-drop guarantee is structural: the send operation enqueues the value with the sender's goroutine state — there is no code path where a send returns without the value being committed to the channel (receiver's stack, buffer slot, or the panic). Contrast languages where queues have offer/try modes returning success flags — Go's send is a statement, not a question, and its return IS the commitment.

select with default is the non-blocking probe built into the language, and its mechanics matter: select locks ALL its channels, checks every case for readiness, and if none is ready AND a default exists, runs default — atomically, under all the locks. The try-send built this way is race-free: two goroutines both doing select-default-send on the same full channel — one wins the single free slot, the other takes default, with no lost or duplicated values, because the whole check-and-commit is under the channel locks.

That composition — one guaranteed-delivery primitive (the send) plus one atomic choice primitive (select) — generates every messaging policy: drop-when-busy (default), wait-then-drop (time.After), first-available (plain select across channels). The pattern to recognize in code review: any 'I need best-effort delivery' requirement maps to select+default over a buffered channel, and the buffer size IS the explicit tolerance for how far ahead the producer may run before losses start. The system's lossiness becomes a number you chose — not a default the runtime chose for you.
